name: Mizuna
summary: Mizuna forms a dense rosette of crisp stems and serrated leaves. It is a cool-season leafy green harvested as baby leaves or at fuller growth; some varieties and production methods support repeat cuts, but regrowth is not a universal household guarantee.

identity.short: Mizuna type within Brassica rapa; infra-specific names vary
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Brassica rapa and treats B. rapa var. nipposinica and subsp. nipposinica as synonyms. USDA GRIN records B. rapa subsp. nipposinica and cites the cultivated Mizuna Group. Penn State uses the var. nipposinica name; Oregon State places mizuna within B. rapa, although one figure caption says B. juncea. The profile therefore uses B. rapa for the mizuna type, records the infra-specific names as nomenclatural context, and does not claim a named cultivar.

growth.short: Dense rosette with crisp stems and deeply serrated leaves
growth.guidance: Penn State describes long, thin, crisp stems and highly serrated leaves growing in rosettes. Oregon State describes dense plants with a mild peppery flavor. These are mizuna-type characteristics, not dimensions or performance claims for a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Cool-season crop; full sun favors growth, partial shade is tolerated
cultivation.guidance: Penn State recommends well-drained, organic-rich soil. Mizuna tolerates partial shade but grows best in full sun (at least six outdoor hours in that guidance), tolerates light frost and is slow to bolt. Supplemental irrigation is advised when rainfall is inadequate. These outdoor recommendations do not define indoor grow-light settings or hydroponic compatibility.

pruning.short: Choose whole-plant or cut-and-come-again harvest
pruning.guidance: For baby-leaf production, Johnny's advises cutting above the basal plate to allow regrowth. Penn State also describes cutting the plant near the ground for a single harvest. These are distinct harvest goals; do not apply the commercial baby-leaf cutting schedule as a home-system guarantee.

harvest.short: Harvest at baby-leaf or full-leaf stage; repeat cuts can regrow
harvest.guidance: Penn State describes harvest from baby greens through full maturity and allows either cutting the whole plant near the ground or cutting at least about 2 inches above the ground for regrowth. Johnny's commercial baby-leaf guide describes 3–6 inch harvest leaves and repeat cuts about 5–14 days later depending on variety and season; that interval is a production reference, not a guaranteed household schedule. Both leaves and stems are edible; young leaves suit salads, while cooked greens work in stir-fries, soups and stews.

problems.short: Cool weather delays bolting; monitor for brassica flea-beetle damage
problems.guidance: Penn State describes mizuna as tolerant of light frost and slow to bolt. Oregon State notes that brassica flea beetles produce small shot holes in leaves and that floating row cover can protect crop establishment; this is regional, crop-group guidance rather than a claim of mizuna-specific susceptibility or resistance.

hydroponics.short: A controlled DWC study tested the named 'Red Hybrid' selection
hydroponics.guidance: A 2025 University of Tennessee/NASA study grew the named 'Red Hybrid' mizuna selection in a controlled environment with a short deep-water-culture phase. This is evidence for that cultivar in that experiment, not for every mizuna type or any Garden appliance. Its experimental light, EC, pH and nutrient conditions are not household recommendations; hydroponic suitability for this broader catalog type remains unknown.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: A controlled study supports only the named 'Red Hybrid' selection in its tested DWC setup; it does not establish hydroponic suitability for the broader Mizuna type or any Garden system.

name: Tatsoi
summary: Tatsoi is the low-rosette type of Brassica rapa, with thick, dark-green spoon-shaped leaves and a mild flavor. It can be grown for baby leaves or as a mature rosette; cited cool-season guidance is regional, and indoor/hydroponic suitability remains unestablished.

identity.short: Tatsoi is the low rosette type of Brassica rapa
identity.guidance: Oregon State places tatsoi in the B. rapa Narinosa group and describes it separately from mizuna and mustard greens. This record represents the tatsoi type, not a named cultivar.

growth.short: Low, flat rosette with thick spoon-shaped leaves
growth.guidance: Oregon State describes tatsoi as a low, flat rosette with thick, spoon-shaped, dark-green leaves and a mild flavor used in East Asian cooking. This type description does not supply a single mature size for every selection.

cultivation.short: A leafy brassica represented in regional cool-season production
cultivation.guidance: Oregon State includes tatsoi among winter leafy greens for western Oregon and Washington and advises growers to follow variety-specific supplier instructions. This regional field/high-tunnel context does not establish a universal home calendar, indoor light tier or hydroponic suitability.

pruning.short: Baby-leaf cutting can preserve regrowth above the basal plate
pruning.guidance: For baby-leaf brassica production, Johnny's recommends cutting above the basal plate; its harvest window and repeat-cut interval depend on variety and season. This method describes baby-leaf use and should not be treated as a full-size tatsoi harvest prescription.

harvest.short: Harvest leaves as baby greens or use the mature rosette
harvest.guidance: Johnny's baby-leaf production guidance includes tatsoi among the brassicas harvested when leaves reach about 3–6 inches, cutting above the basal plate for possible repeat harvests; the next cut varies with variety and season. Oregon State describes the mature type as a low rosette with spoon-shaped leaves but does not provide a universal household harvest size or schedule.

problems.short: Watch for shot-hole feeding on brassica leaves
problems.guidance: Oregon State describes flea beetles as producing shot-hole damage on brassica leaves and says floating row cover can protect establishment. This is brassica-group guidance for a regional production context, not evidence of tatsoi-specific resistance or a diagnosis of any single damaged leaf.

name: Mustard Greens
summary: This identity represents Brassica juncea mustard greens, not every plant sold under the variable common name. Leaf shape and pungency differ among types; young leaves are harvested tender, with cool-season timing varying by region. UF/IFAS documents crop-level adaptability to multiple hydroponic systems, but not compatibility with a specific Garden unit or cultivar.

identity.short: Mustard greens is a variable group; this identity represents B. juncea
identity.guidance: Oregon State warns that the common name mustard greens covers diverse species, subspecies and hybrids, with substantial naming confusion. This Garden identity retains Brassica juncea and the general mustard-green type recorded in its taxonomy; it should not be read as covering every crop sold under a mustard-greens name or a named cultivar.

growth.short: Leaf form and pungency vary across mustard-green types
growth.guidance: Oregon State describes B. juncea as ranging from more pungent forms to crops grown for broad or swollen petioles and tender flowering stems. Those differences reflect the group's diversity; this profile does not assign an unrecorded leaf shape, cultivar or flavor intensity to the general identity.

cultivation.short: Cool-season leafy crop; outdoor timing varies by region
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension includes mustard greens among cool-season crops for fall gardens and notes light-frost tolerance in its Minnesota context. OSU's western Cascades guide treats mustard greens as a diverse group and recommends checking variety-specific supplier instructions. These outdoor sources do not establish indoor lighting; see the separately scoped UF/IFAS hydroponic evidence below.

pruning.short: Cut baby leaves above the basal plate when regrowth is intended
pruning.guidance: Johnny's baby-leaf guide includes baby mustard among brassicas suitable for cut-and-come-again harvest. It recommends cutting above the basal plate; this describes commercial baby-leaf production and is not a universal pruning rule for mature mustard-green types.

harvest.short: Young leaves can be harvested before full size; succession extends supply
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension notes that small mustard leaves are tenderer and tastier than fully grown leaves and suggests successive plantings every few weeks for a steady supply. For baby-leaf production, Johnny's describes cuts at about 3–6 inches above the basal plate, with repeat timing varying by variety and season. These are crop-group references, not a fixed cultivar maturity date.

problems.short: Monitor for flea-beetle shot holes on brassica greens
problems.guidance: Oregon State describes flea beetle feeding as shot-hole damage on brassica foliage and notes that floating row cover can protect establishment. Johnny's also lists flea beetles and cabbage worms/loopers for commercial baby-leaf brassicas. These are group-level risks; no disease resistance or identity-specific susceptibility is established here.

hydroponics.short: UF/IFAS documents mustard greens across multiple hydroponic systems
hydroponics.guidance: UF/IFAS identifies mustard greens as Brassica juncea and says the crop adapts to multiple hydroponic systems. It also warns that summer or hot-greenhouse conditions can trigger bolting. This supports crop-level hydroponic feasibility, not compatibility with every household appliance, cultivar-specific performance, or a nutrient recipe.

conditions.description: UF/IFAS describes Brassica juncea mustard greens as adaptable to multiple hydroponic systems; this does not validate every household appliance or layout.
UF/IFAS reports bolting in summer or hot-greenhouse conditions; environment affects suitability.

evidence.note: Florida protected-culture guidance explicitly describes mustard greens as adaptable to multiple hydroponic systems; no specific Garden model or nutrient-engine mapping is inferred.

name: Collard Greens
summary: Collards are a leafy, non-heading Brassica oleracea crop type harvested as tender leaves or whole plants. Utah State Extension supports selective older-leaf harvest that can permit continued growth; exact dimensions and any named-cultivar performance remain unspecified.

identity.short: Collard Greens is resolved at Brassica oleracea and Collard type type scope
identity.guidance: Collards are a leafy, non-heading Brassica oleracea crop type. The selected sources support crop-level harvesting and outdoor context; no named cultivar, mature dimensions or cultivar-specific performance is asserted.

growth.short: Large edible leaves; no compact head is formed
growth.guidance: Utah State Extension treats collards with other leafy brassica greens harvested as leaves or whole plants, rather than as a heading crop. UF/IFAS reports collard stems averaging nearly 3 ft at maturity and sometimes reaching 6 ft over time; these are broad crop references, not dimensions for a named cultivar or a compact system. Leaf yield still depends on selection and conditions.

cultivation.short: Outdoor crop guidance; hydroponic production is documented but not every system fits
cultivation.guidance: USU's crop guidance is for field-grown collard and other brassica greens. UF/IFAS documents collards in outdoor hydroponic troughs but warns that robust growth may not suit every system. These sources do not map outdoor light to a grow-light tier or establish a Garden appliance configuration.

care.short: Harvest older leaves while preserving active younger growth
care.guidance: USU reports that individually removing older collard leaves can allow continued plant growth. This is crop-level field harvest guidance; it does not promise a fixed number of repeat cuts in a home or indoor system.

pruning.short: Manage by harvest, thinning, and visible crowding
pruning.guidance: Routine shaping cuts are not established for this unspecified collard type. Remove older leaves as harvest, and remove damaged tissue when needed; do not infer a container or hydroponic pruning schedule.

harvest.short: Pick tender leaves individually or harvest the whole plant
harvest.guidance: USU describes hand-harvesting collard greens either by cutting the plant at the base or removing older individual leaves so the plant can continue growing. Harvest stage depends on intended use; the source's commercial timing is not assigned to this identity.

problems.short: Inspect for leaf-feeding insects and sap-feeding pests
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS identifies leaf-feeding beetles and caterpillars (including cabbage loopers, diamondback moth larvae, armyworms, cutworms and cabbage webworms), as well as aphids, whiteflies and stink bugs, as collard pests. The page does not provide a symptom key for each pest or establish cultivar-specific susceptibility; inspect plants and confirm identification before choosing an intervention. UF/IFAS recommends integrated pest management rather than indiscriminate treatment.

thinning.short: Thin or separate according to the intended harvest form
thinning.guidance: USU publishes row-spacing guidance for field collards, but it is not a Garden pod-spacing recommendation. Do not infer a one-plant-per-pod rule without a system-specific source.

hydroponics.short: Collards have been grown hydroponically, but robust size limits system fit
hydroponics.guidance: UF/IFAS shows Flash collards in an outdoor hydroponic system and cautions that not all systems suit the crop; staking and removal of dead leaves may be needed to manage stems and canopy. This is crop-level evidence for some hydroponic production, not a guarantee for compact appliances, a pod-count rule, or a nutrient recipe.

evidence.note: UF/IFAS documents hydroponic collard production but explicitly warns that not every system fits this robust crop; no compact-machine compatibility is claimed.

name: Red Cabbage
summary: A red cabbage identity in Brassica oleracea. The available crop guidance supports cool-season head formation, steady moisture, harvest at usable head size and common head-quality concerns, but not a specific cultivar or color-performance claim.

identity.short: Red cabbage is a horticultural type within Brassica oleracea
identity.guidance: UW–Madison lists Red Acre and Red Danish among specialty cabbage cultivars. This catalog identity represents red cabbage as a type and does not select either cultivar or claim a particular red-cabbage seed line.

growth.short: Head-forming cabbage; no cultivar-specific dimensions established
growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes cabbage heads as overlapping leaves and notes that head shape varies. The source does not establish this identity's particular head size, color intensity or cultivar, so those remain unspecified.

cultivation.short: Cool-season crop; steady moisture supports firm heads
cultivation.guidance: Cabbage grows best in cool weather. UMN's home-garden guidance describes fertile, well-drained yet moisture-retentive soil and steady water/nutrient uptake; its pH, dates and outdoor soil advice are regional crop guidance, not an indoor or hydroponic prescription.

pruning.short: Protect the young central growing point; routine shaping is not established
pruning.guidance: UMN Extension notes that damage to the central growing point while cabbage is small can prevent head formation. Avoid injuring it during handling or maintenance; the source does not call for routine pruning.

harvest.short: Cut a firm head once it reaches a useful size
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension advises harvesting cabbage when the head reaches a usable size, cutting above the outer leaves. Mature heads can split, especially after heavy rain, so assess the head and local conditions rather than waiting for a fixed date.

problems.short: Uneven moisture, head splitting or central-point damage can affect quality
problems.guidance: UMN Extension links inconsistent water with poor head texture and notes splitting after heavy rain or once heads mature. Damage to a young central growing point can prevent head formation. These are crop-level risks, not diagnoses or cultivar-specific susceptibility claims.

name: Brussels Sprouts
summary: Brussels sprouts form a sequence of compact buds along a tall leafy Brassica oleracea stalk, beginning at the lower leaf axils and progressing upward. Consistent soil moisture supports tight, tender sprouts; cooler autumn weather can improve flavor, but Minnesota season guidance is regional.

identity.short: Sprout-forming type of Brassica oleracea
identity.guidance: UMN describes Brussels sprouts as compact heads of tender leaves forming along the stalk of a tall leafy plant. This is crop/type evidence; it does not establish the mature dimensions or cold tolerance of a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Keep soil moisture consistent as sprouts develop
cultivation.guidance: UMN notes that Brussels sprouts need consistent soil moisture for tender, tight, well-flavored buds; dry spells can leave sprouts loose, poorly formed, or bitter. Its weekly watering quantity and fall calendar are Minnesota soil-garden guidance, not a universal system setting.

growth.short: Sprouts develop in leaf axils from the bottom upward
growth.guidance: Each sprout forms where a leaf joins the main stem, starting low and continuing upward. A tall stalk with many large leaves is normal; small sprouts should not be mistaken for a single compact cabbage head.

pruning.short: Topping is optional and tied to lower-sprout development
pruning.guidance: UMN suggests cutting off the growing top after the lowest sprouts reach about one inch to encourage upper sprouts to enlarge. This is a conditional management option from regional guidance, not a required pruning rule or cultivar-specific guarantee.

harvest.short: Pick developed sprouts along the stalk; cool weather can improve flavor
harvest.guidance: Sprouts enlarge from the bottom upward. Harvest developed lower sprouts as needed or cut and store the stalk when the crop is mature; UMN reports that cool fall weather improves flavor. Its frost thresholds and storage schedule are regional and not cultivar-specific.

problems.short: Dry spells affect sprout texture; rotate the cabbage family
problems.guidance: Inconsistent moisture can produce loose, poorly developed, bitter sprouts. UMN also lists several cabbage-family diseases and recommends a four-year rotation away from cole crops to reduce disease carryover. Disease pressure varies; this is prevention guidance, not diagnosis or cultivar resistance.

name: Kohlrabi
summary: Kohlrabi is a cool-season Brassica oleracea grown for a swollen stem that forms above the soil, not for a root bulb. Harvest it while crisp and tender; oversized stems can become woody, and the leaves are also edible.

identity.short: Kohlrabi is an enlarged-stem type of Brassica oleracea
identity.guidance: UMN identifies kohlrabi as Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes and describes the edible swollen stem above ground. The Garden identity retains species-level naming and kohlrabi type; no named cultivar is represented.

cultivation.short: Cool-season growth with steady moisture and fertile, drained soil
cultivation.guidance: UMN describes best quality under cool conditions and steady growth without heat or moisture stress, in fertile soil that retains moisture but drains well. The stated 65–75°F range and regional soil recommendations are crop guidance, not a cultivar-specific indoor or hydroponic prescription.

growth.short: The edible swollen stem sits above the soil surface
growth.guidance: The bulb-like portion is an enlarged stem formed just above the ground, topped by upright leaves; it is not an underground root. UMN also notes that the leaves can be eaten as cooked greens.

pruning.short: No routine pruning protocol is documented
pruning.guidance: The cited home-garden guide does not prescribe routine pruning. Keep the developing stem visible and avoid burying or damaging it during cultivation; this is a practical handling adaptation, not a cultivar-specific growing rule.

harvest.short: Harvest the stem while it is still crisp and tender
harvest.guidance: UMN gives 2–3 inches across as a regional harvest cue and warns that larger kohlrabi can become tough, woody and bitter. Treat size as a guide rather than a universal cutoff; the leaves are edible too.

problems.short: Heat, drought, and oversized stems reduce quality
problems.guidance: UMN reports that rapid growth without heat or moisture stress supports good quality, while oversized stems can turn tough, woody and bitter. These are crop-level quality cues, not a disease diagnosis or a named-cultivar trait.

name: Patio Tomato
summary: Patio tomato refers to dwarf or semi-dwarf forms selected for a tidy, short habit that can suit containers. It is a growth-type label rather than one cultivar: actual plant size, determinate/indeterminate behavior, support and pruning depend on the named seed variety.

identity.short: Patio tomato is a dwarf/semi-dwarf growth type, not a single cultivar
identity.guidance: Johnny's describes patio tomatoes as dwarf or semi-dwarf plants with a tidy habit and short stature, generally suitable for container culture. The catalog keeps this as a horticultural type within Solanum lycopersicum; it does not assign a named cultivar or exact mature dimensions.

growth.short: Tidy, short-statured habit; size still varies by named variety
growth.guidance: The patio/dwarf label points to smaller, tidier growth compared with full-size vining tomatoes, but Johnny's notes dwarf forms can themselves be determinate or indeterminate. No universal height or spread is assigned to this type record; use the exact seed variety's dimensions when available.

cultivation.short: Containers may fit the type, but match the pot to the exact variety
cultivation.guidance: Johnny's identifies patio/dwarf tomatoes as generally appropriate for container growing. UMN's general tomato guidance still applies to outdoor growth: warmth, full sun and a long frost-free season. The type-level source does not specify a universal pot size, indoor-light setting or hydroponic system fit.

care.short: Container moisture needs attention, but the type has no fixed watering interval
care.guidance: Iowa State notes that container tomatoes can dry quickly and recommends watering thoroughly through a freely draining medium without letting it dry completely or remain waterlogged. This is tomato-in-container guidance, not a universal pot size, amount, schedule or hydroponic reservoir instruction for every patio variety.

pruning.short: Do not infer support or pruning needs from 'patio' alone
pruning.guidance: Dwarf forms may be determinate or indeterminate. Check the exact seed variety: determinate types often need little pruning, while an indeterminate dwarf may still need support and selective shaping. This type identity does not establish a universal pruning schedule or promise that every plant can stand unsupported.

harvest.short: Harvest timing and fruit cues belong to the named variety
harvest.guidance: The patio label does not define a single fruit size, color or days to maturity. UMN advises harvesting tomatoes at usable size and color; consult the chosen variety's description for its expected ripe color and maturity estimate.

problems.short: Watch container moisture and diagnose fruit disorders before intervening
problems.guidance: UMN links tomato fruit cracking and blossom-end rot with uneven soil moisture during fruit growth. This is general tomato guidance; the patio-type sources do not demonstrate greater disorder risk in containers or a particular cultivar. Check the growing medium and visible fruit symptoms before changing care.

flowering.short: Flower movement supports fruit set; sustained heat can cause flower drop
flowering.guidance: At crop level, UMN Extension explains that tomato flower parts sit close together and flower movement can transfer pollen; tomatoes can produce fruit without bee pollination. UMN's Minnesota-specific example says sustained days above 85°F and nights above 70°F can stress flowers and impair fruit set; flowers may then drop. Treat this as regional diagnostic context, not a trait of every patio variety or indoor setpoint.

name: Sun Gold Tomato
summary: Sun Gold F1 is an indeterminate cherry tomato with exceptionally sweet, tangerine-orange fruit. Johnny's lists about 57 days from transplant and notes a tendency to split, so it is best treated as a fresh-use tomato rather than a shipping type.

identity.short: Sun Gold F1 is a named indeterminate orange-cherry cultivar
identity.guidance: Johnny's identifies Sun Gold as an F1 Solanum lycopersicum with indeterminate growth. Its supplier description specifies bright orange cherry fruit; those characteristics belong to Sun Gold, not to tomato or cherry types generally.

growth.short: Vigorous, season-long vine with 15–20 g orange cherries
growth.guidance: Johnny's describes vigorous plants that begin yielding early and continue through the season, bearing bright tangerine-orange fruit around 15–20 g each. These are the supplier's product characteristics; mature plant dimensions are not established here.

cultivation.short: Warmth, full sun and a frost-free outdoor season
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension describes tomatoes as heat-loving and requiring full sun and a long frost-free season. This is outdoor crop-level guidance, not a Sun Gold temperature threshold, indoor-light target or hydroponic prescription.

care.short: Even soil moisture helps protect fruit quality
care.guidance: UMN Extension links consistent soil moisture with tomato fruit quality and advises against overhead watering because wet foliage is more disease-prone. This is soil-garden guidance, not a Sun Gold-specific water volume or reservoir interval.

pruning.short: Support the continuing vine; do not manage it like a bush tomato
pruning.guidance: As an indeterminate tomato, Sun Gold continues growing and fruiting over an extended period. Johnny's recommends staking, trellising or caging indeterminate tomatoes; its general guide describes selective sucker pruning as an option, not a rule to remove every shoot. Set support before the vine becomes difficult to handle.

harvest.short: Pick fully colored fruit as it ripens; 57 days is a supplier estimate
harvest.guidance: Johnny's lists 57 days to maturity from transplant for its Sun Gold product and describes early, repeated ripening. Use the deep orange color and ripe-fruit feel as cues; the stated interval varies with transplant age, weather and growing conditions and is not a days-from-sowing promise.

problems.short: Fruit splitting is a known Sun Gold limitation
problems.guidance: Johnny's notes that Sun Gold tends to split and is not suited to shipping. UMN Extension explains that tomato growth cracks are associated with rapid fruit growth and swings in soil moisture, often after dry periods followed by heavy rain or watering. Keep soil moisture more even when growing in soil; do not diagnose every split as disease or transfer this soil advice to a reservoir schedule.

flowering.short: Flowering and fruit set continue on the indeterminate vine
flowering.guidance: Johnny's describes Sun Gold as bearing through the season. Track flowers, fruit set, ripening clusters and split fruit as distinct observations; a temporary pause in fruit set can reflect conditions and should not be labeled disease without diagnosis.

uses.short: A fresh-market cherry for eating fresh
uses.guidance: Johnny's describes Sun Gold as an exclusively fresh-market treat because ripe fruit tends to split and does not ship well. Its sweet, fruity flavor suits fresh eating; no universal shelf-life or storage duration is inferred.

name: Supersweet 100 Tomato
summary: Supersweet 100 F1 is an indeterminate red cherry tomato that bears 15–20 g fruits in large clusters. Johnny's lists about 60 days from transplant and reports resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and Verticillium wilt for its named product.

identity.short: Supersweet 100 is a named F1 cherry tomato
identity.guidance: Johnny's identifies Supersweet 100 as an F1 Solanum lycopersicum. The cultivar's fruit, maturity and resistance notes below are scoped to that supplier's named product and are not generic cherry-tomato traits.

growth.short: Indeterminate vine with red fruit in large clusters
growth.guidance: Johnny's describes a vigorous, reliable cherry tomato with clusters of red fruit around 15–20 g each. It is indeterminate, so the vine continues to grow and set fruit over an extended period; this does not supply a measured mature height or spread.

cultivation.short: Warmth, full sun and a frost-free growing season
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension describes tomatoes as heat-loving plants requiring full sun and a long frost-free season. These are general outdoor tomato conditions, not a Supersweet 100 temperature threshold, indoor-light target or hydroponic prescription.

care.short: Keep soil moisture steadier while fruit develops
care.guidance: UMN Extension links fluctuating soil moisture during fruit growth with disorders such as cracking and blossom-end rot, and recommends watering soil rather than foliage. These are garden-soil practices, not a measured water volume or reservoir schedule for this cultivar.

pruning.short: Support the vine; use pruning selectively rather than by a fixed rule
pruning.guidance: Johnny's identifies this cultivar as indeterminate. Its tomato guide recommends staking, trellising or caging vining tomatoes and describes removing low suckers beneath the first strong branch as a possible management approach. The profile does not prescribe aggressive pruning; retain enough healthy foliage to support fruit and respond to the actual structure.

harvest.short: Harvest clusters as the red cherries ripen; 60 days is a transplant estimate
harvest.guidance: Johnny's lists about 60 days from transplant and says fruit ripens gradually from the blossom end and along the cluster. Pick fruit at the intended ripe stage; days vary with conditions, and this estimate is not measured from sowing.

problems.short: Listed resistance is product-specific, not immunity
problems.guidance: Johnny's lists high resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and Verticillium wilt for its Supersweet 100 F1 seed product. Resistance does not mean the plant cannot become diseased and does not cover other pathogens. For visible symptoms, identify the issue before treatment; UMN notes that tomato disorders and diseases can look similar.

flowering.short: Watch flower-to-cluster set through the long harvest window
flowering.guidance: Because Supersweet 100 is indeterminate and produces fruit in large clusters, follow flower clusters through fruit set and ripening instead of expecting one synchronized crop. Record flower drop separately from disease symptoms; the sources do not support a single cause without observation.

uses.short: Sweet red cherry for fresh eating
uses.guidance: Johnny's describes Supersweet 100 as a classic sweet red cherry with high yields and fruit produced in clusters. That supports fresh-snacking use; it does not establish that the cultivar is the best choice for every recipe or storage method.

name: Celebrity Tomato
summary: Celebrity is a semi-determinate slicer tomato: University of Florida IFAS classifies the cultivar between bush and vining habits, while Delaware Extension lists red, globe-shaped fruit around 7–8 oz. Treat those fruit details and regional maturity references as source-specific, not universal guarantees.

identity.short: Celebrity is a named Solanum lycopersicum cultivar
identity.guidance: University of Florida IFAS identifies Celebrity as a semi-determinate tomato cultivar. The catalog's word 'type' does not imply that all Celebrity-branded lines or Celebrity Plus share identical traits; named forms must stay distinct.

pruning.guidance: UMN Extension says removing old blooms promotes new flowers. It suggests pinching to encourage bushier growth when stalks cannot support flower heads; it does not make pinching a universal rule for every zinnia habit.

flowering.short: Large dahlia-type blooms; repeated cutting is reported for Johnny's mix
flowering.guidance: Johnny's describes its State Fair Mix as producing 3–5 in double and semi-double dahlia-type flowers in a variable color mix and calls it cut-and-come-again. Treat this as the vendor's product-level description, not a guarantee for every supplier's offering or a claim of cultivar-specific pollinator performance.

harvest.short: Cut flowers for repeat harvest; bloom-stage guidance differs by production context
harvest.guidance: Johnny's describes its State Fair Mix as cut-and-come-again. For general zinnia handling, Rutgers advises cutting when flower centers just begin to open, using clean tools and hydrating stems quickly; Mississippi State's farmer-florist guide describes harvesting fully developed blooms and retaining two to three leaf pairs. These are different crop-level production contexts, not State Fair-specific trials. Choose the stage for the intended bouquet/production goal; no single State Fair-specific harvest stage or vase-life guarantee is established.

problems.short: Watch for powdery mildew; no State Fair disease resistance is established
problems.guidance: UMN Extension reports powdery mildew as a common zinnia concern and recommends dry foliage and good airflow. Mississippi State describes whitish or gray powdery leaf surfaces as a symptom. This supports crop-level monitoring only; no resistance or susceptibility claim is made for the State Fair mix.

name: Viola / Pansy
summary: Garden pansy (Viola × wittrockiana) is a low, rounded cool-season flowering hybrid suited to beds and containers. Iowa State recommends full to part sun, moist well-drained soil and steady watering; light freezes are tolerated, while summer heat can sharply reduce performance. Indoor and hydroponic suitability remain unestablished.

identity.short: Garden pansy hybrid, Viola × wittrockiana; no named series is represented
identity.guidance: Iowa State and Texas Tech identify garden pansy as Viola × wittrockiana. This profile represents the pansy horticultural type, not every Viola species, horned violet, Johnny-jump-up, color pattern or named commercial series.

growth.short: Rounded, mounded plants with large, variable-color flowers
growth.guidance: Iowa State describes pansies as rounded and mounded, typically about 4–10 inches tall with a similar spread; Texas Tech reports about 4–8 inches tall and 8–12 inches wide. The references differ modestly and describe horticultural ranges, not a guarantee for an unnamed series.

cultivation.short: Cool-season outdoor crop; keep soil moist but well drained
cultivation.guidance: Iowa State recommends full to part sun, with part sun useful when temperatures are warm, and moist, well-drained soil. Keep plants watered during dry weather; a light fertilizer can benefit container plants. Iowa planting dates and summer behavior are regional, not a universal calendar or indoor-light prescription.

pruning.short: Remove faded flowers to encourage continued flowering
pruning.guidance: Texas Tech's pansy profile recommends deadheading faded flowers for continued bloom. No cultivar-specific pruning schedule or hydroponic response is established.

flowering.short: Performs in cool seasons; heat can end the display
flowering.guidance: Iowa State describes pansies as cool-season annuals that tolerate light freezes and provide spring or fall color in Iowa. It reports that many decline or 'melt' in hot Iowa summers; timing is regional and modern series vary in heat performance.

harvest.short: Ornamental bloom; Texas Tech lists pansy flowers as edible
harvest.guidance: Texas Tech lists pansy flowers as edible but provides no preparation method or cultivar-specific food quality. This profile therefore makes no recipe or medicinal claim.

problems.short: Watch heat stress, root rot, anthracnose and slugs
problems.guidance: Iowa State lists occasional root rot, anthracnose and slug problems and identifies hot weather as the most consistent limitation. These are monitoring concerns, not a diagnosis or a disease-resistance rating for an unnamed pansy series.

name: Plumosa Celosia
summary: Plumosa celosia is the feathery-plume horticultural type of Celosia argentea, grown for cut and dried flowers. NC State's species guidance supports full sun and well-drained soil, while Mississippi State's cut-flower guidance describes the Plumosa type's day-length response and says routine pinching is unnecessary. Flowering timing and dimensions vary by selection and production context; hydroponic fit remains unestablished.

identity.short: Accepted species Celosia argentea; Plumosa is a horticultural type, not a named cultivar
identity.guidance: POWO treats Celosia argentea var. plumosa as a synonym of the accepted species C. argentea. Mississippi State Extension uses the var. plumosa name for its cut-flower guidance. Garden retains the accepted species plus Plumosa type and does not assign a named series or cultivar.

growth.short: Feathery plume inflorescences on well-branched stems
growth.guidance: Mississippi State describes plume heads about 3–12 inches long on 12–48-inch stems in cut-flower production. These wide production ranges reflect selection and growing context; they are not a guaranteed home-garden mature size for an unnamed series.

cultivation.short: Full sun and drained soil; production flowering also responds to day length
cultivation.guidance: NC State's species-level Celosia argentea profile recommends full sun and amended, well-drained soil and says the species tolerates heat and humidity. Separately, Mississippi State's Plumosa cut-flower guidance reports faster flowering at photoperiods of 14 hours or less and longer stems under longer days. These are outdoor species and commercial-production contexts, not an indoor grow-light recipe or hydroponic protocol; field spacing is not converted to a Garden pod count.

pruning.short: Routine pinching is not required for Plumosa celosia
pruning.guidance: Mississippi State says pinching is not necessary for celosia and distinguishes cockscomb forms, for which it recommends pinching. Do not transfer that cockscomb-specific branching advice to the Plumosa type.

flowering.short: NC State describes bloom from late spring to frost; timing is not a local guarantee
flowering.guidance: NC State's general C. argentea profile lists bloom from late spring to first frost and describes the Plumosa Group's feathery plume form. Mississippi State's separate cut-flower guidance explains that photoperiod changes flowering speed and stem length in production. Neither source establishes a calendar for a particular packet or unnamed series.

harvest.short: Cut fresh stems when the plumes are fully developed; dry at the same stage
harvest.guidance: For cut-flower production, Mississippi State recommends harvesting fresh or dried stems when flowers are fully developed. For drying, remove foliage and hang stems in a dark, well-ventilated location. Published vase-life and storage values depend on cultivar and commercial handling, so none is assigned to this unnamed type.

problems.short: Avoid crowded, persistently wet conditions; monitor for production pests
problems.guidance: NC State warns that crowding, rain and high humidity can cause flower rot and that root rot is possible; it also mentions slugs/snails in landscape settings. Mississippi State's cut-flower guidance lists aphids and thrips and describes powdery mildew as white powdery growth on leaves and sometimes flowers. These are scoped monitoring cues, not a diagnosis or a resistance claim.

name: Rutabaga
summary: Rutabaga is a Wave 2 baseline identity with crop/type guidance. Exact cultivar performance, system response, and dimensions remain scoped to the cited evidence.

identity.short: Rutabaga is resolved at Brassica napus and Rutabaga type type scope
identity.guidance: Rutabaga is Brassica napus, distinct from turnip (Brassica rapa). This record represents the rutabaga crop/type, not a named cultivar; turnip traits are not transferred to it.

cultivation.short: Grow the storage root through summer into cool fall weather
cultivation.guidance: UMN and USU Extension describe rutabaga as a cool-season crop whose roots need time to develop and mature in cool weather; Utah guidance treats it as a fall crop. Both recommend sunny sites and deep, fertile, well-drained soil. These are outdoor regional crop recommendations, not a named-cultivar or hydroponic specification.

growth.short: Dense storage root; distinguish it from the smaller, tender turnip
growth.guidance: UMN describes rutabagas as Brassica napus with typically denser, harder roots than turnips, commonly yellow-fleshed and generally cooked. This is crop-level context, not a guaranteed color or texture for every named selection; the profile keeps rutabaga distinct from Brassica rapa turnip.

care.short: Avoid drought and moisture swings while the root is sizing
care.guidance: Both UMN and USU warn that inconsistent water can impair root quality; UMN notes drought stress can make roots bitter or woody, while USU also identifies cracking, woody roots and pithiness. Their regional water amounts differ (about 1 inch/week in UMN guidance versus 1–2 inches/week in USU guidance), so use local weather and soil rather than treating either number as a universal schedule.

harvest.short: Harvest in fall; a light frost can improve flavor
harvest.guidance: UMN advises leaving rutabagas in the ground into September or October and notes that flavor often improves after a hard frost; USU describes roots around 4 inches and a 60–80-day crop maturity reference. These are regional crop guides, not a fixed cultivar calendar; use root size and local season, then loosen the soil with a digging fork rather than pulling a large root by its tops.

problems.short: Check leaf holes, root tunneling and root disorders before diagnosing
problems.guidance: UMN lists flea beetles that chew small round holes in leaves, root maggots that feed on developing roots, and crop-group diseases including Alternaria leaf spots, black rot and clubroot. These are warning signs and possible causes, not a diagnosis of an individual rutabaga; confirm the symptom and growing context before choosing management.

name: Broccoli Raab
summary: Broccoli raab (rapini) is a Brassica rapa leafy flowering shoot, not true heading broccoli (B. oleracea). It is harvested for tender leaves, stems and unopened buds; high temperatures can trigger bolting and shorten the tender harvest window.

identity.short: Rapini is a Brassica rapa type, distinct from true broccoli
identity.guidance: UC Master Gardener guidance identifies rapini/broccoli raab with Brassica rapa var. rapa, related to turnip rather than heading broccoli (B. oleracea). The Garden identity stays at Brassica rapa and a horticultural raab type; no named cultivar is asserted.

cultivation.short: Cool-season crop; heat and longer days can trigger bolting
cultivation.guidance: UC Master Gardener describes rapini as a cool-season crop grown to mature in cool weather and notes that high temperatures can trigger flowering. Sonoma County dates are regional; do not reuse them as a universal calendar or as indoor light requirements.

growth.short: The edible harvest includes leaves, stems and flower buds
growth.guidance: Unlike heading broccoli, rapini is grown for tender leafy tops and flowering stems. Small yellow flowers can appear among the buds; this is part of its crop identity, although the most tender harvest is before buds open.

pruning.short: Harvest the shoot rather than shaping it as a broccoli head
pruning.guidance: The source does not give a routine pruning schedule. A careful cut can leave two leaves intact, after which some plants may resprout; this repeat growth is reported as possible, not guaranteed for every plant or system.

harvest.short: Cut tender shoots before buds open
harvest.guidance: UC Master Gardener recommends cutting rapini before the buds open; its Sonoma County guide gives 10–15 inches as a local harvest cue, not a universal threshold. Cut where the stem becomes succulent rather than tough. Leaves, stems and buds are all part of the harvest; leaving two leaves may allow some resprouting.

problems.short: Heat and dry soil can shorten the tender harvest window
problems.guidance: The UC Master Gardener guide reports that rapini bolts in high temperatures and warns that improper watering can contribute to sudden head splitting. These are crop-level regional notes, not a named-cultivar resistance claim. Keep soil from becoming severely dry and inspect buds as temperatures rise.

name: Endive
summary: Endive is a cool-season leafy chicory grown for salad and cooking leaves. Heat, dry spells and bolting can reduce leaf quality; the catalog identity is a horticultural type, not Belgian witloof or a named cultivar.

identity.short: Accepted species Cichorium endivia; general endive type
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Cichorium endivia. This record represents endive as a general leafy horticultural type and does not identify a named cultivar, Belgian witloof (Cichorium intybus), or the distinct broad-leaved escarole record. Crop evidence is kept at its actual species, type, or regional scope.

cultivation.short: Cool-season leafy crop with shallow-root moisture needs
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension groups endive with lettuce and chicory greens: they grow best in cool conditions and have shallow roots that need steady soil moisture. Its temperature ranges, planting calendar and field spacings are Minnesota outdoor guidance; they are not transferred to other climates or indoor/hydroponic systems.
cultivation.context: Crop-group guidance from a Minnesota home-garden source; adjust timing to local conditions.

growth.short: Leafy chicory; endive types include curly forms
growth.guidance: UMN identifies endive among chicories and describes curly endive as a common salad green with mild flavor and slight bitterness. This catalog's general Endive type is not a claim about a particular curly cultivar, Belgian endive, or escarole's broad smooth leaves.

care.short: Keep soil moisture steady; avoid a dry-to-wet swing
care.guidance: UMN notes that these shallow-rooted greens need regular watering; a heavy watering after a dry period can contribute to tipburn. Use soil moisture and leaf condition to guide watering rather than treating Minnesota rainfall guidance as a fixed amount for every garden.

harvest.short: Pick usable leaves or cut the plant before heat-driven bolting
harvest.guidance: UMN recommends harvesting single leaves at usable size or cutting the whole plant at or just above the soil. It warns that heat and long days can cause bolting, strong bitterness and the end of harvest. The timing is crop-level guidance, not a maturity date for an unspecified endive type.

problems.short: Watch for bolting, tipburn and leaf-feeding pests
problems.guidance: UMN reports heat/long-day bolting with marked bitterness, tipburn after moisture fluctuations, and leaf damage from slugs, snails, flea beetles and cutworms across its lettuce/endive/radicchio crop group. These are regional crop-group observations, not a diagnosis or a cultivar-specific susceptibility claim.

thinning.short: Choose spacing by leaf harvest goal; keep it in outdoor-garden scope
thinning.guidance: UMN Extension lists frilly endive at 5 inches for baby-leaf harvest and 10–12 inches for full-size growth; it lists 8 inches when self-blanching is intended. These are Minnesota outdoor soil-garden references for the described endive forms, not a rule for every chicory type or a Garden system position count.

hydroponics.short: Species forms have been grown in a greenhouse floating system
hydroponics.guidance: A peer-reviewed University of Palermo greenhouse trial grew both escarole (Cichorium endivia var. latifolium) and curly endive (var. crispum) in a floating hydroponic system. This supports species-form hydroponic production evidence, but the catalog's general Endive type does not identify a cultivar or establish fit for a Garden X appliance, household pod spacing, or a transferable nutrient recipe.

conditions.description: Evidence is from a controlled greenhouse floating hydroponic trial of escarole and curly-endive species forms; a general Endive entry does not establish household machine compatibility or a cultivar-specific result.

evidence.note: The study includes both var. latifolium (escarole) and var. crispum (curly endive) in a greenhouse floating system; it does not validate a consumer appliance or nutrient settings.
